blocks.text: Chapter 2.
Widen Your Options: Escape "Whether or Not"
Second night, friend — and it opens in 1953, with a president doing arithmetic out loud.

Dwight Eisenhower, the general who ran D-Day, stands before the nation and prices a single modern bomber — not in dollars, but in alternatives: one bomber, he says, costs the equivalent of modern schools in more than thirty cities. Or two fully equipped hospitals. Listen to what he did there, friend: "should we build the bomber or not?" is the narrow question. Bomber-versus-schools is the real decision. Every choice spends resources that could have gone somewhere else — and the somewhere-else almost never gets a seat at the table.
Tonight: the first villain — narrow framing — hunted on its home ground, and the tools that blow the frame wide open.
The smoke alarm phrase

Listen to how people describe their hardest decisions: "Should I break up with him or not?" "Should we fire this employee or not?" "Should I buy the car or not?" Each sounds like a decision, friend — but it isn't one yet. It's a referendum: a single option put to an up-or-down vote with every other possibility left offstage. Baruch Fischhoff coded teenagers' real decisions and found roughly 65% involved no real alternatives at all. And before we smile at the teens — recall from last night that 71% of organizational decisions were the same single-option votes. As researcher Dan Lovallo quipped: most businesses make decisions like hormone-addled teenagers.

Pause and guess: Paul Nutt tracked his database of real organizational decisions for YEARS afterward, checking which choices were still in place and considered successful. He split them into "whether or not" decisions versus decisions weighing two or more genuine alternatives. What were the long-term failure rates?
Ready? Here is what happened.

"Whether or not" decisions failed 52 percent of the time. Decisions with two or more real alternatives failed just 32 percent. One additional genuine option cut the long-run failure rate by more than a third, friend. Three mechanisms do the work: comparing options teaches you the landscape — what you're trading away — which sharpens your judgment of every option including the first; alternatives give you a scouted fallback when Plan A stumbles; and multiple options loosen ego's grip — with one proposal on the table, its sponsor defends it like a personal cause; with several, people can abandon a weakening option without losing face. And note how low the bar is: not ten options — the paralysis of too much choice is a real but overrated worry — just from one to at least two. Most decisions, personal and corporate, fail to clear even that. So build the alarm, friend: whenever you hear "whether or not" — from yourself or anyone — the decision is not ready to be made. The right response isn't to deliberate harder. It's to ask the prior question: what else could we do?
The genie's only trick

Knowing you should generate alternatives is easy; doing it is hard, because the current option monopolizes your attention. The Heaths' crowbar is the vanishing options test: imagine a genie appears and declares that every option you're currently weighing has been erased from the universe. You cannot choose any of them. Now what do you do?

It sounds like a parlor trick, friend, and it works like a charm — because it converts "evaluate this option" into "solve this problem," and people are far better problem-solvers than they realize. They just never get asked. The Heaths tell of a manager stuck on "fire Anna the receptionist, or not?" — Anna being good with customers, sloppy with details, prickly with colleagues. Vanish both options and the manager immediately produced what no one had voiced: give Anna direct feedback and a chance to improve; redesign the role around her strengths; move the detail work; hire a part-timer for the gaps. Any of those might beat both original "options" — and none surfaced until the originals were forcibly removed. The student asking "break up or not?" is choosing between two blurry bundles; vanish both and better questions appear: what specifically is missing — is it fixable — what would a trial separation reveal? Two notes, friend: take the genie seriously — really pretend the options are gone — and use it before you're desperate. Scarcity of options is usually an illusion created by attention. The genie's only magic is forcing your spotlight to move.
The five-word nudge

Now the cheapest widening tool ever measured. Economist Shane Frederick was shopping for a stereo — torn between a $1,000 Pioneer and a $700 Sony — when a bystander reframed it: "the Pioneer... or the Sony plus $300 of albums?" The fog lifted instantly. So Frederick ran the experiment.

Pause and guess: Participants were asked if they'd buy a $14.99 video of a favorite actor. Group one chose between "buy" and "don't buy." Group two's second option added five words that tell shoppers NOTHING they don't already know: "don't buy — keep the money for other purchases." What happened to the purchase rate?
Ready? Here is what happened.

It fell from 75 percent to 55 percent. A phrase containing zero new information made a fifth of buyers reconsider, friend — which tells you exactly how narrow our frames run: even a nudge toward the blindingly obvious widens them. That's opportunity-cost thinking in one habit: for any expenditure — money, headcount, calendar hours — name the specific next-best use of the same resources, and make it an explicit competing option. A $20,000 project isn't competing against nothing; it's competing against everything else $20,000 could do. Eisenhower's bomber against thirty towns' schools. And then interrogate the "or" itself, friend, because many either/ors are false: Steve Cole at HopeLab needed a device built and — rather than picking one vendor — split the first phase among several, small bets that let him compare real performance instead of proposals. His rule of thumb deserves a card of its own: "Is there a way I can do this AND that?" Surprisingly often there is — especially when you shrink the initial commitment.
Before you go

So: "whether or not" is a smoke alarm, not a decision; one extra real option cuts failure by a third and frees egos to fold; the genie's vanishing test turns evaluators back into problem-solvers; five obvious words cut purchases by a fifth, because our frames are that narrow; and the best answer to either/or is often and — in miniature. This week, friend: catch one "whether or not" in the wild — yours or a colleague's — and refuse to proceed until a second genuine alternative sits beside it.

But two options raise tomorrow's question: how do you explore several roads without tripling the work or dithering forever? The Heaths' answer comes from an unlikely lab — design firms racing deadlines, and one banana company in a crisis — plus the single most useful shortcut in decision-making: finding someone who has already solved your problem. Next time: multitrack — and find your someone.
Key takeaways
"Whether or not" is a referendum, not a decision — 65% of teen choices and 71% of corporate ones consider no real alternative.
Nutt's ledger: single-option decisions fail 52% long-term; two-plus alternatives fail 32% — one more option cuts failure by a third.
Alternatives teach the landscape, scout your fallback, and let sponsors abandon weakening options without losing face.
The vanishing options test: erase every current option and solve the problem — attention, not reality, was hiding the menu.
Opportunity cost is nearly free: "keep the money for other purchases" cut buying 75%→55% — always name the next-best use.
Interrogate the "or": shrink the commitment and ask whether you can do this AND that.
